activitySchema.heading: Read the marks before choosing a challenge
activitySchema.instruction: Label A, B and C. Match each study to the line structure you can see. A technique is an option to try, not your assigned challenge.

items.label: A
items.feedback: The parallel lines have wider gaps, so more of the white paper remains visible.

items.label: B
items.feedback: The parallel lines are closer together. Their spacing differs from A.

items.label: C
items.feedback: Two sets of lines cross. This is cross-hatching, rather than a single set of parallel strokes.

activitySchema.discussion: Try a relevant technique beside your own baseline. Point to its actual effect, then choose a skill that serves your own artistic intention.

diagram.alt: Three original line studies. A has widely spaced parallel lines. B has closer parallel lines. C has two crossing sets of lines.
diagram.caption: Original classroom studies. Label what is visible; choose your own artistic intention in the practical trial.

activitySchema.heading: Order a layout test in the plan
activitySchema.instruction: Order this four-step thumbnail test. Use each position once. The purpose comes first and both small sketches are kept.

items.label: Compare where the eye goes in the two sketches.
items.feedback: Compare the actual arrangements against the focus you intended.

items.label: Name the intended focus of this layout test.
items.feedback: A clear intention gives the comparison a purpose.

items.label: Choose the next step and keep a reason with both sketches.
items.feedback: Use the comparison to decide whether to keep or adjust the planned action.

items.label: Make two small arrangements of the same shapes.
items.feedback: Thumbnails let you test an arrangement before adding detail.

activitySchema.discussion: Try a step from your own plan. Include its resources, time and support. If the trial reveals a missing step, update your plan from what happened.

activitySchema.heading: Predict a hatching change, then test it
activitySchema.instruction: Predict before making the next patch. Keep the original patch. Check the model reason, then compare the actual marks.

items.label: The pencil, paper and light pressure stay similar. What might closer line spacing do?
items.feedback: Closer lines leave less white paper between them and can create a darker tone. Check your real samples from the same distance.

options.label: Create a darker tone while retaining line texture.
Make a lighter tone because less white paper is visible.

items.label: Paper, pencil, pressure and spacing all change. Can the result isolate spacing alone?
items.feedback: The art may be useful, but several changes prevent that single-cause conclusion.

options.label: Yes; the darker sample proves spacing caused it.
No; several features changed at once.

items.label: Your actual patch differs from your prediction. What belongs in the process record?
items.feedback: The real difference helps you decide a next trial. A prediction must not replace the observed work.

options.label: Both real patches and what you noticed.
Only the result that you expected to see.

activitySchema.discussion: Use the trial to refine your own challenge. Preserve the earlier state, record your decision and keep any outside comment attributed.

activitySchema.heading: Spot an unsupported review claim
activitySchema.instruction: Spot the error in these practice claims. Choose a repair that keeps a real artistic example, your own view and the evidence of sharing distinct.

items.label: “I noticed the slow opening pace. That proves the whole audience wanted to make art.”
items.feedback: Your observation can support your own account of an artistic effect. It does not establish everyone else’s creative response.

options.label: Describe your own response and the observed detail.
Keep the whole-audience claim because it sounds positive.

items.label: “My final review is saved in a folder, so another person has received it.”
items.feedback: Saving and sharing are different actions. Record a recipient and evidence only after the final review has actually been communicated.

options.label: A saved filename proves the review was shared.
Keep sharing open until someone actually receives the review.

items.label: “It was good because it was good” is the complete review.
items.feedback: Add a real artistic feature, its effect and your own creative impact. Your judgement may be positive, mixed or critical.

options.label: Use a specific artistic example and explain its impact on you.
Repeat the same judgement in a longer sentence.

activitySchema.discussion: At the actual arts experience, attend as an audience member through the agreed access route. Use real notes for your final review and its actual share. If the experience has not happened, label this preparation.

activitySchema.heading: Keep the research strands distinct
activitySchema.instruction: Sort the five example records by their stated main purpose. These are record types, not facts about a named person or evidence that your own encounter happened.

items.label: A real workshop sample and note identify the practitioner, the meeting and the task I personally tried.
items.feedback: This can record a first-hand encounter when the named meeting and activity really occurred.

items.label: A checked arts-centre page explains its role and who can take part.
items.feedback: This answers an organisation question. It does not replace meeting a practitioner.

items.label: A provider’s current course page states skills taught and entry requirements.
items.feedback: This is an education route. Check the real source and access details before treating it as available.

items.label: A practitioner’s actual account describes an arts work role and the skills it involves.
items.feedback: This informs a career route, without guaranteeing work or earnings.

items.label: My own account explains how something I explored affects my next arts choice.
items.feedback: This records influence in the pupil’s own words, supported by a real finding.

activitySchema.discussion: Meet practitioners through the arranged first-hand workshop or event. Then check your real encounter, organisation, education and career sources. Explain the influence yourself and leave missing contact or research open.

activitySchema.heading: Keep two reviewers’ voices
activitySchema.instruction: Everyone commits before we compare. Choose what each example can support. The final judgement concerns your actual arts challenge.

items.label: A person says “looks great” without looking at the aim or changes. What is still needed?
items.feedback: The comment may encourage you, but a review should concern the real challenge and give a clear view linked to the work.

options.label: Nothing; any positive comment completes the outside review.
Their own review of the actual aim, process and result.

items.label: The outside reviewer sees progress, but the pupil still finds one transition abrupt. What should the record keep?
items.feedback: Both views may be supported by different details. The pupil explains their own judgement without changing the other review.

options.label: Both real views, with the work and each person’s reasons.
Only the more positive view so the records agree.

items.label: An adult supplies a completed paragraph and the pupil has not confirmed its meaning. Is it the pupil’s final review?
items.feedback: Prompts and exact scribing can support the pupil’s own account. An unconfirmed adult judgement cannot replace it.

options.label: Yes, because it is saved in the pupil’s part file.
No; gather and confirm the pupil’s own judgement.

activitySchema.discussion: Ask for the actual outside review, then make your own final review. Keep their locations separate. A missing reply stays a next action.

activitySchema.heading: Annotate a role in the planning sketch
activitySchema.instruction: Label A, B and C. This example aims to show the whole artwork with a separate caption, checked from the viewing place.

items.label: A
items.feedback: The caption covers part of the left image. That conflicts with this example’s stated aim to show the whole work.

items.label: B
items.feedback: The right caption is separate from the artwork. Its actual readability still needs a check.

items.label: C
items.feedback: This is the viewing position. A caption that is legible at the desk may need a different size or position here.

activitySchema.discussion: Name a decision you could lead in your own arts project and how it serves the shared aim. Agree your responsibility with others; the planning sketch itself is not leadership-delivery evidence.

categories.label: Caption covering part of the image
Place to check the viewer’s experience

activitySchema.heading: Connect each practical choice to its purpose
activitySchema.instruction: Sort the example planning choices by their main purpose. No invitation, booking or feedback collection is claimed to have happened.

items.label: Draft the message explaining the print activity and how to ask about joining.
items.feedback: Promotion explains the opportunity. The draft remains unsent preparation.

items.label: Use the agreed invitation route and check which willing learners can attend.
items.feedback: Recruitment concerns the actual people and their responses; do not assume attendance.

items.label: Count the usable print tools and available backing sheets.
items.feedback: This resource check helps you choose a feasible scale or plan turns.

items.label: Plan a place for wet work that keeps the walking route clear, with staff checking the arrangement.
items.feedback: This addresses a practical risk. An entry in a plan is not proof that the real setup has been checked.

items.label: Plan to ask which choice helped a participant make their pattern.
items.feedback: The feedback question links to the arts purpose. A response is recorded only when it is given.

activitySchema.discussion: Now make your own five-area plan. If the group or tools change, revisit all affected choices, including access, timing and who needs to agree.

activitySchema.heading: Predict a clearer instruction, then ask
activitySchema.instruction: Predict before a willing collaborator tries the instruction. Keep the original. Check the actual response without supplying it for them.

items.label: The wording and viewing place stay the same, but the letters become larger. What is a fair prediction?
items.feedback: Larger letters may be easier to see. The collaborator’s actual response tests the prediction; size alone does not ensure understanding.

options.label: The larger letters may be clearer from that place.
The larger letters must solve every access difficulty.

items.label: The collaborator says both versions are already clear. What does the trial show?
items.feedback: Keep the true response. You do not need to manufacture a problem or claim an improvement that was not observed.

options.label: The larger version improved it, regardless of their reply.
This person found both versions clear in this trial.

items.label: You change the words, letter size and position together. What can you conclude?
items.feedback: A combined change may help the task, but the test does not isolate letter size. Explain the limit when updating the plan.

options.label: We must check the whole change and cannot isolate letter size.
Any improvement proves letter size alone caused it.

activitySchema.discussion: Test an actual project step with the team. Agree the action and your own contribution. Keep rehearsal and preparation distinct from real delivery.

activitySchema.heading: Spot the gap in a delivery claim
activitySchema.instruction: Spot the error in each statement. Choose a record or action that fits what actually happened in the arts project.

items.label: “Everyone joined in because all their names were on my plan.”
items.feedback: A plan names intended participation. Actual attendance and actions must come from the delivery record.

options.label: Record who actually took part and what happened.
Use the plan as proof of every person’s participation.

items.label: “Time is short, so I will finish the participant’s artwork without asking.”
items.feedback: Leading supports another person’s choices. Offer a feasible step or agreed help, and keep any unfinished work honest.

options.label: Take over their work so the project looks complete.
Ask what help they want and agree a manageable next step.

items.label: “The finished artwork alone proves every leadership decision I made.”
items.feedback: The outcome and the leadership process show different things. Add a factual record of actual actions and your own explanation.

options.label: Link the outcome to my actual actions, decisions and responses.
Claim every planned decision from the final image.

activitySchema.discussion: Carry out your own agreed role in real delivery when ready. Keep rehearsal labelled and never replace participants’ choices with evidence-making.

activitySchema.heading: Choose a respectful check before adapting
activitySchema.instruction: Everyone commits before we compare. Choose what the observation supports, then plan a check within your agreed role.

items.label: A participant pauses after the tool moves. What do you know?
items.feedback: The pause is observable. Its meaning needs a respectful check rather than a guess about the person.

options.label: They must dislike the activity.
They paused; I can ask which step or support they need.

items.label: Someone asks to see the first fold again. Which response leaves the making choice with them?
items.feedback: Show the requested action and check their real response. Repeating a step is not permission to finish their work.

options.label: Show that fold on scrap and invite them to try.
Fold their whole piece before they can respond.

items.label: The team checks the current method and finds it works for this phase. Must the leader change it?
items.feedback: Keeping a method for an evidence-based reason is a valid decision. Record the check and any remaining limits.

options.label: Yes; every comment must lead to a visible change.
No; keep it for a reason and record the actual check.

activitySchema.discussion: Use a real project response. Agree any change with the responsible people, keep the earlier state and check the effect with others.

activitySchema.heading: Order a shared display task
activitySchema.instruction: Put this agreed small display task in order. Use each place once. Hear both views before assigning or fixing the pieces.

items.label: Each person carries out the part they agreed.
items.feedback: Do your own part and tell the collaborator if something changes.

items.label: Check the display together from the actual viewing place.
items.feedback: Agreement is checked against the result. Name any remaining action.

items.label: Hear both views and check what the collaborator means.
items.feedback: Listening gives the agreement a real basis; do not write someone’s reply in advance.

items.label: Agree who places the image, who places the caption and what support is needed.
items.feedback: Responsibilities need agreement. A shared task should still make each person’s contribution identifiable.

activitySchema.discussion: Carry out your real project task with your collaborator. Ask before changing their work, keep your own contribution clear and link it to an earlier example of teamwork.

activitySchema.heading: Separate judgement, evidence and next step
activitySchema.instruction: Sort these example review cards. All concern the teacher’s paper-form example, not a claim about your project.

items.label: “Moving the model made my explanation clearer for the person who asked.”
items.feedback: This interprets what the event meant. It needs the actual response to support the judgement.

items.label: “The feedback says: I could see the fold once it moved.”
items.feedback: The quoted response is evidence for this person’s experience, not the whole group’s learning.

items.label: “Before another session, I would check the view from each place.”
items.feedback: This is a reasoned future action. It has not already been tested.

items.label: “My project note records that I moved the model after a request.”
items.feedback: A true project note records the action. Its location lets the reader check the account.

activitySchema.discussion: Test one judgement in your own review against the real record. Separate your contribution from the group result, keep feedback attributed and choose a reasoned next step.

activitySchema.heading: Locate three different evidence roles
activitySchema.instruction: Label A, B and C on the two-unit map. Match the marked part to the evidence it needs, then follow an actual locator in your own work.

items.label: A
items.feedback: Part 1B holds the personal arts-challenge practice, another person’s review and the pupil’s final review. Leadership work cannot replace it.

items.label: B
items.feedback: Part 2C concerns effective arts leadership in real delivery, with the pupil’s actual role and decisions.

items.label: C
items.feedback: Part 2E is the pupil’s evidence-based review of the leadership project. A plan is not a completed review.

activitySchema.discussion: Check all nine parts, not just these three. Open the actual files and pages, slides or timecodes. Count the full Silver file set against the existing cap of 20; label real gaps instead of filling them with examples.
